title: When Disaster Strikes, Could AI Help? Q&A with Jessica Jensen
gist: RAND's Jessica Jensen finds a surprisingly large market of 1,179 AI-enabled emergency-management tools, but says the market is skewed toward disaster response over preparedness/recovery, is fragmented into narrow single-purpose products creating a 'stacking problem,' and that adoption is blocked more by organizational capacity, connectivity, and pricing opacity than by a lack of available technology.

insights.claim: A RAND study (supported by the Markle Foundation's AI for Disasters + Emergencies Initiative) identified 1,179 AI-enabled products relevant to emergency management, far more than the researchers expected going in.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
entities: AI for Disasters and Emergencies Initiative
insights.so_what: Signals a much larger and more fragmented emerging vendor market in disaster-tech AI than commonly assumed — relevant for investors scouting govtech/public-safety AI consolidation plays.
insights.quote: We were shocked by the number of tools out there. We thought we might find dozens. Instead, we found 1,179.

insights.claim: The AI emergency-management tool market is skewed heavily toward disaster response (situational awareness, hazard monitoring, damage assessment, information sharing) with comparatively few tools built for preparedness or recovery phases.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: Identifies an underserved product gap (preparedness/recovery-phase AI tools) as a potential white space for new entrants or targeted investment.
insights.quote: But the market is uneven, with more tools for response than for preparedness or recovery.

insights.claim: Jensen's team identified a 'stacking problem': most AI products in emergency management deliver only one narrow piece of insight and don't integrate with other information streams, forcing organizations to buy, connect, and manage multiple disconnected tools themselves.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: A named, reusable framework ('stacking problem') for evaluating fragmentation risk in any narrow-vertical AI tool market — a company that solves integration/interoperability has a clear wedge.
insights.quote: Many offer one piece of insight, but they do not connect different information streams or help create a fuller picture. That creates what we call a stacking problem.

themes.theme: Adoption barriers are organizational, not technological

insights.claim: Jensen argues the core adoption barrier is not tool availability but whether emergency-management organizations have the internal capacity to evaluate, purchase, integrate, and sustain use of these tools over time.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the common 'more tools = more capability' narrative — vendors targeting this market should prioritize implementation/support services over feature proliferation.
insights.quote: As we found, it's not that the tools do not exist. It is whether organizations have the capacity to evaluate them, buy them, integrate them, and keep using them over time.

insights.claim: Many AI emergency-management products require dedicated IT expertise to set up and maintain, but many local jurisdictions lack that staffing; many products also require internet connectivity that can fail during an actual response, and pricing is often opaque, complicating procurement.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: A checklist of concrete product-design flaws (connectivity dependence, opaque pricing, IT-heavy setup) that any vendor or investor should screen for when assessing disaster-tech AI vendors' real addressable market.
insights.quote: Many products also require internet connectivity, which can become an issue during response. A significant number depend on another product to work. And pricing is often hard to find—which makes procurement difficult.

insights.claim: Jensen frames the path to wider AI adoption in emergency management as requiring three simultaneous shifts: technology companies designing more field-specific products with transparent pricing, policymakers reforming governance/procurement/funding rules, and emergency managers building more familiarity with the tools' capabilities and limits.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: A three-part adoption framework (vendor transparency, policy reform, buyer literacy) transferable to other public-sector AI procurement contexts beyond disaster management.
insights.quote: Technology companies can design products more specifically for this field and prioritize transparency on pricing, access, and technical requirements—which will drive better adoption.
insights.locator: Q&A on what it will take for wider adoption

insights.claim: Jensen says general-purpose large language models and chatbots are the AI tools most likely to deliver quick wins in emergency management today because they are broadly capable, user-friendly, and already accessible to some jurisdictions for administrative tasks like summarizing reports, drafting materials, and translation.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: Suggests off-the-shelf LLM products (not bespoke disaster-AI systems) are the near-term adoption path for cash-strapped public-sector buyers — relevant to enterprise LLM vendors targeting government.
insights.quote: We found they could be especially useful for administrative and communication tasks in emergency management. They can help summarize reports, draft materials, translate information, and process large amounts of text more efficiently.
insights.locator: Q&A on the role of LLMs

insights.claim: For more complex emergency-management tasks beyond administrative work, Jensen says there is still insufficient research and real-world testing to determine whether LLMs are effective.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations for near-term LLM deployment in mission-critical (as opposed to administrative) disaster-response functions — a caution for over-hyped claims about AI operational autonomy in crisis response.
insights.quote: For more complex emergency management tasks, though, there is still more research and real-world testing that needs to be done to determine LLMs effectiveness.
insights.locator: Q&A on the role of LLMs

insights.claim: AI could shift emergency managers' time away from routine desk work (plans, outreach materials, grant management) toward public-facing work like community relationship-building and disaster-impact mitigation, according to Jensen.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
insights.so_what: A concrete labor-reallocation thesis for AI in public-sector roles — administrative automation freeing staff for higher-value human-relationship work, a pattern seen across many white-collar AI adoption cases.
insights.quote: AI can speed up much of that work. That allows emergency managers to spend less time behind their desks and more time doing important public-facing work.
insights.locator: Q&A on realistic AI use cases

themes.theme: Role of philanthropy in fast-moving tech fields

insights.claim: Jensen argues philanthropic funders' most valuable role in fast-moving AI fields is convening technology companies, user communities, and researchers to negotiate competing interests, which she says is what differentiates tools that merely sound promising from tools that actually help communities.
insights.speaker: Jessica Jensen
entities: AI for Disasters and Emergencies Initiative
insights.so_what: A transferable model for how philanthropic capital can de-risk early-stage AI-for-good markets by funding coordination rather than just funding the technology itself.
insights.quote: That convening role—and the ability to sustain those conversations—can make the difference between tools that sound promising and tools that actually help communities.
